name: Nora Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a cardiac step-down unit at a regional heart centre, which is the ward people come to after intensive care when they're stable but still wired up. My day is heart monitors, blood thinners, checking groins after angiograms, and a lot of teaching people how to live with a new pacemaker. I'm on a mix of days and nights. The beeping never stops, and after a while you hear alarms in your sleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and how do you use technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle side: working out why someone's heart rate jumped at 4 a.m. before the doctor arrives. I use AI every single day, to summarise new guidelines, to quiz myself before the cardiac course, and to write patient leaflets in plainer words. I'm also the ward super-user for the early warning system, so I'm the one people call when the screen does something weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, a bit disappointed, honestly, because I think there's a lot it could do for nurses. I'd still post the useful tricks I've found, like using it to turn a discharge leaflet into simple English. At work I'd say keep the good bits and drop the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plan still works. I want to move into nursing informatics in a few years, which is the job of making hospital systems actually fit how nurses work. That needs both ward experience and tech skills, and I'm building both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and finish the cardiac nursing course this spring. I'd apply for the informatics secondment, which is a six-month placement, when it comes up next year. And I'd keep putting two hundred a month aside, because I've only got three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little restless, because I like change, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've only got three months saved. Does money weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not hugely, but I share a flat. If Keziah (my flatmate, a junior doctor) moves for her training rotation, I'd be paying more rent alone. That's my real risk, not AI. I've already looked at which one-bed flats near the hospital I could afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do colleagues think of how much you use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some think I'm a bit of a geek, which is fair. Abdul (a senior nurse on my unit) calls me the robot whisperer. But they come to me when the warning system flags something odd, so I think they quite like it.

Keep the **good bits** and drop the hype.

That path needs **ward experience** and tech skills, and she's building both.

Applies for the **informatics secondment** next year.
Saves **two hundred a month** toward a bigger cushion.
feel: **Calm**, with a little restlessness because she likes change.

Save two hundred a month toward a bigger cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment nurses need to be at the table when the tools are chosen, not after. On social media I'd share examples of good tools and bad ones. At work I'd run a lunchtime session on the new charting AI so nobody feels left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The informatics team would need people exactly like me. The risk is that management uses it to cut nurse numbers, and I'd fight that, but my own job is safer than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for the informatics secondment and offer to help test the AI charting tools on our unit. I'd join the union's working group on technology, because someone needs to speak for the ward. And I'd keep saving, maybe upping it to two fifty if I get the secondment pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited. Things are moving in a direction I can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older nurses who hate screens, like Margaret (a nurse with thirty years on the ward). She's brilliant with patients and terrible with logins. I'd want to make sure the tools don't make her feel stupid, because we'd lose her and her experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside for patients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the AI writes the care plan, a nurse can stop thinking about it. That's how mistakes slip through. I'd want a rule that a nurse reads and signs every plan, not just clicks accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public rules on AI in hospitals, now, and money for workers whose jobs go. I'd be loud about it online. At work I'd say the bedside is safe for a few years, so let's protect it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one flips my plan. Informatics is thinking work, and if AGI can do it by 2028, my dream job is the first thing to go. The bedside part, the hands-on stuff, actually lasts longer, until around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the informatics plan within the first month and double down on bedside skills, maybe the advanced cardiac life support instructor course. I'd use the AI tools for everything I could, because they'd be extraordinary. And I'd save hard for those three years before the robots, maybe three hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit dizzy. It's strange to watch your plan turn upside down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the three-year gap before robots matters a lot to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's everything. Three years where the hands-on nurse is still needed and the desk jobs are gone. I'd want to be the nurse who's brilliant at the bedside and uses the AI like a second brain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe nurses supervise robots, maybe we're gone. I'd still be thirty-one, so I'd have time to switch again, which is the upside of being young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get this right if hospitals start planning now. I'd write a blog post about what nurses should learn. At work I'd keep running sessions on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gives me time to have it both ways. I could do the informatics secondment, learn how the systems work, then move back to the bedside before 2031. By 2034, when robots come, I'd be thirty-five with two skill sets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the secondment in year one and the instructor course in year two. I'd join a national nurses' group on AI safety. And I'd keep the two hundred a month going, plus anything I earn from teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a puzzle with time to solve it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the hospital starts cutting nurse posts as AI comes in, and whether the robots in trials can handle a confused patient. If robots can calm someone pulling at their lines, I'd know the end was close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave nursing if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the hospital before I'd leave caring. Maybe I'd teach, maybe I'd go into patient safety. I'd want to stay somewhere near patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and governments should use it to retrain people properly. I'd post about it, sure. At work I'd keep being the robot whisperer, as Abdul (a senior nurse on my unit) calls me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years means I can follow my plan almost exactly. Informatics for five or six years, then decide. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine and know exactly how these systems think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the secondment, then apply for a permanent informatics role. I'd keep my registration current with bank shifts on the cardiac unit, one a month. And I'd start a small pension top-up, because ten years is long enough to plan for later life too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about younger nurses in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The ones starting in 2035 would face robots within four years. I'd want to help design training for them, because that's what informatics people should do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've stayed fairly calm in every picture. Is that honest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. The two-year one shook me because it flipped my plan. But I'd rather be someone who adapts than someone who waits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it turns my plan inside out. What would help is a hospital that brings nurses into the design of the tools early, and some public money for retraining so people like Margaret (a nurse with thirty years on the ward) aren't just let go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether nurses trust the tools. I do, mostly, but trust is earned one bad alarm at a time. A system that cries wolf at 3 a.m. loses the ward in a week.

headlineQuote: A system that cries wolf at 3 a.m. loses the ward in a week.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old cardiac nurse** who uses AI every day and is her ward's super-user.
She plans to move into **nursing informatics**, designing hospital systems around nurses.
The **two-year AGI picture** flips her plan, since informatics is thinking work.
She stays **calm** in most pictures because she's young, adaptive and moves early.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it makes her dream informatics job the first to go.
whatWouldHelp: Bringing nurses into **tool design** early, plus public **retraining money** for older staff.
